strengths: Addresses a practically important problem with non-curated, reward-free offline data across multiple embodiments
Comprehensive evaluation on 72 tasks with consistent improvements (102.8% relative improvement), substantially more than prior work
Clear problem diagnosis using t-SNE visualization and Wasserstein distance analysis (Figure 2) to motivate distributional shift issue
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating contribution of each component (pre-training, experience rehearsal, execution guidance)
Strong reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, full results tables, and computational resources disclosed
Practical techniques that are straightforward to implement and integrate with existing methods
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core techniques (experience replay, behavioral cloning, RSSM pre-training) are well-established; main contribution is combining existing methods rather than developing fundamentally new approaches

Overclaimed 'non-curated' data characterization: data is still in-domain and task-specific (DMControl/Meta-World), collected from pre-trained RL agents with specific noise injection, undermining claims of being arbitrary non-curated data
Unfair experimental setup: baselines receive preprocessed data containing only task-relevant trajectories while GSA leverages full multi-embodiment dataset, making comparisons not entirely clean
Shallow theoretical analysis: Propositions 1-3 in Appendix B are straightforward (mixture distributions, coupled policy analysis follows standard TRPO), lacking deep or novel theoretical insights

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: limited analysis of which aspects of offline data contribute most to improvements, why simpler approaches might not work equally well, or detailed failure case analysis
Generalization concerns: simulation-only evaluation, acknowledged challenges with new embodiments/configurations, unclear scalability beyond manipulation/locomotion tasks
Limited sensitivity analysis: many hyperparameters (mixing ratio 0.25, execution guidance schedule, retrieval threshold k) lack thorough ablation studies
Task adaptation experiment (Section 4.2) uses only one baseline and simplified continual learning setting, somewhat disconnected from main contribution

strengths: Extensive experimental evaluation on 72 tasks (12× more than typical RL papers) with strong aggregate improvements of 102.8% over learning-from-scratch baselines
Clear problem identification with effective visualization of distribution shift (Figure 2) using t-SNE plots and Wasserstein distances
Comprehensive baseline comparisons across multiple categories: training-from-scratch, offline-leveraging, model-based, and continual learning methods
Practical relevance to leveraging abundant non-curated offline data for improved RL sample efficiency
Well-structured presentation with detailed appendices including implementation details, theoretical analysis, and full results tables
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (trajectory retrieval from RLPD/ExPLORe, behavioral cloning similar to JSRL, standard RSSM architecture) without fundamental innovation

Critical fairness concerns with baseline implementations: authors explicitly modify ExPLORe (replacing RND with ensembles, sharing latent space) after failing to reproduce original performance, raising serious credibility questions about comparisons

Misleading characterization of 'non-curated data': claimed in-the-wild data is actually in-domain, carefully collected via TDMPC v2 agents and curiosity-driven RL; authors acknowledge in Appendix D that generalization to new embodiments is 'still challenging'
Unequal data access in comparisons: GSA receives full multi-embodiment diversity while baselines are preprocessed to only task-relevant trajectories, making direct comparison problematic

Weak theoretical contributions: Proposition 1 trivially follows from selecting nearby states; Proposition 2 is standard regularization; Proposition 3 relies on strong TRPO assumptions. Propositions add minimal novel insight

Insufficient component analysis: paper identifies distribution shift but doesn't isolate which components drive improvements or how much each contributes beyond 'more training data'; ablations limited to 4 tasks

Ad-hoc execution guidance design: task-dependent schedules (different linear() parameters for DMControl vs Meta-World) with random mid-episode switching lacks principled justification and sensitivity analysis

Concerning result patterns: many Meta-World tasks still have low success rates (Assembly 0.2, Hand Insert 0.4); some regressions vs longer-horizon baselines (Faucet Close 0.8 vs 1.0); high task variance masks generalization
Reproducibility challenges: 280M parameter model requiring 1728 GPU hours with 30+ hyperparameters for tuning; modified baseline implementations complicate reproduction and comparison

Limited analysis depth: no trajectory-level retrieval strategy justification (Eq. 4 uses only initial observations); no world model prediction accuracy analysis; missing statistical significance testing despite only 3 seeds

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation on 72 visuomotor tasks—12x more than prior world model baselines, providing valuable evidence for the approach
Clear problem diagnosis: identifies distributional shift between offline and online data during fine-tuning (Figure 2) and effectively motivates the solutions
Practical problem formulation addressing reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data—more realistic than prior work assuming curated rewards
Thorough ablation studies isolating contributions of each component (Figures 6-8) with additional comparison to uncertainty-based alternatives (OTS)
Consistent improvements across diverse tasks including hard exploration scenarios where learning-from-scratch baselines fail significantly
Well-executed experimental methodology with appropriate baselines, multiple seeds, and informative visualizations
Straightforward and practical techniques (retrieval-based experience rehearsal via Faiss, behavioral cloning guidance) that are easy to implement
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: experience rehearsal is conceptually similar to RLPD/ExPLORe, execution guidance mirrors JSRL, and world model uses standard RSSM—primarily combines existing techniques rather than introducing novel methods

Fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: baselines receive only task-relevant trajectories while GSA uses full multi-embodiment data, creating asymmetric data access that confounds algorithmic contributions

Misleading framing of 'non-curated' data: remains in-domain (DMControl/Meta-World), comes from structured sources (unsupervised and pre-trained RL agents), and artificial quality variation via noise injection

Weak theoretical contributions: Proposition 1 is intuitive (retrieving similar states reduces distribution shift), Proposition 2 restates known regularization results, Proposition 3 applies standard TRPO bounds without novelty

Insufficient analysis of failure cases and limitations: poor performance on certain tasks (Pick Place, Reach, etc.) lacks explanation; generalization to new embodiments acknowledged but unaddressed; task-specific execution guidance scheduling suggests limited generality

No real-world validation: all experiments simulation-only; acknowledged gap ('We only conduct experiments in the simulator') undermines practical claims and sample efficiency benefits may not transfer

Missing computational analysis: no breakdown of costs for pre-training (48h), retrieval, behavioral cloning training; world model size (280M parameters) impact unexplored; hyperparameter sensitivity not studied

strengths: Comprehensive large-scale empirical evaluation across 72 visuomotor tasks with consistent improvements (~2× over baselines at 150k samples)
Well-motivated practical problem: leveraging reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data is realistic and valuable
Clear problem analysis with effective visualization of distributional shift between offline and online data (Figure 2)
Strong reproducibility: complete algorithm, implementation details, hyperparameters, and extensive ablation studies provided
Successfully learns task-agnostic world model across 6 embodiments, demonstrating multi-embodiment scalability
Intuitive techniques that address identified issues: experience rehearsal mitigates distributional shift, execution guidance encourages exploration
weaknesses: Limited novelty: experience rehearsal and execution guidance are incremental variations of RLPD/ExPLORe and JSRL-BC respectively; world model uses standard RSSM with minor modifications
Mixed results on pre-training effectiveness: Figure 6 shows pre-training alone degrades performance on Meta-World tasks, contradicting core motivation without adequate explanation

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: paper identifies distributional shift but doesn't deeply explain why simply mixing retrieved offline data solves this; no analysis of what world model learns across embodiments
'Non-curated' data is still algorithmically curated (curiosity-driven RL agents, TDMPC with controlled noise) and in-domain; overstates the non-curation aspect

Experimental setup concerns: baselines receive task-relevant preprocessing while NCRL uses full multi-embodiment data (information advantage); different random seeds (5 vs 3) and no statistical significance testing
Retrieval quality issues: Table 2 shows 84%/68% precision on some tasks; Figure 14 shows robustness to 75-100% task-irrelevant data, undermining claimed retrieval benefits
Weak theoretical contributions: Proposition 1 is straightforward (retrieved data is closer by definition); Proposition 2 merely applies Kakade & Langford (2002) with no novel insight
Simulation-only evaluation with acknowledged limitations on generalization to unseen embodiments/tasks; no real-world experiments despite claiming practical benefits

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 72 tasks with 5 random seeds, substantially more than related work like iVideoGPT
Addresses practical problem of leveraging reward-free, unlabeled offline data for RL
Clear problem diagnosis with visualization of distributional shift between pre-training and fine-tuning (Figure 2)
Strong empirical results achieving ~2x aggregate score compared to learning-from-scratch baselines at 150k samples
Extensive ablation studies showing contribution of each component
Detailed reproducibility information and hyperparameters provided
weaknesses: Severely limited technical novelty: world model pre-training is standard RSSM (Hafner et al.), experience rehearsal is straightforward retrieval+replay, execution guidance is essentially JSRL with minor modifications
Theoretical contributions are trivial: Proposition 1 is obvious (selecting closer samples reduces distance), Proposition 2 is direct application of Kakade & Langford (2002)
Fundamentally mischaracterized problem: data claimed as 'non-curated' is actually in-domain and highly structured (100% retrieval precision on most tasks, Table 2)
Unfair baseline comparisons: baselines receive task-relevant-only filtered data while NCRL uses ~100x larger full dataset; unclear if aggregate results (Fig 3) control for this

Weak evidence that proposed techniques drive improvements: Figure 6 shows pre-training alone provides most benefits; unclear whether gains come from more pre-training data or the fine-tuning techniques
iVideoGPT aligned comparison (Fig 10) shows only marginal NCRL superiority, questioning whether improvements stem from techniques vs. data quantity
Unclear mechanisms: execution guidance claims to 'steer toward high-confidence regions' but no explicit mechanism provided; comparison with uncertainty-based rewards (Fig 7) limited to 2 tasks
Insufficient design choice justification: no ablation on retrieval metrics, execution guidance schedule differs by task (suggesting hyperparameter tuning), no analysis of retrieved set size
Limited generalization: only in-domain data tested; authors admit inability to leverage in-the-wild data; no cross-embodiment transfer studied; simulation-only experiments despite robotics framing

Statistical concerns: NCRL uses 5 seeds vs 3 for baselines, potentially biasing variance estimates; Figure 14 shows robustness to 100% task-irrelevant retrieved data, which raises questions about whether retrieval is crucial

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation on 72 diverse visuomotor tasks with clear empirical improvements (~2× over learning-from-scratch baselines at 150k samples)
Well-motivated problem identification: distributional shift between offline pre-training and online fine-tuning data is clearly demonstrated (Figure 2) with concrete evidence
Practical problem formulation addressing realistic constraints (reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment data) rather than idealized settings
Thorough ablation studies showing contribution of each component, hyperparameter sensitivity, robustness to data quality degradation, and impact of fine-tuning different world model components
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters (Table 6), full algorithm (Algorithm 1), computational requirements, and comprehensive appendices
Strong baseline comparisons against multiple state-of-the-art methods (DrQ-v2, DreamerV3, R3M, UDS-RLPD, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, iVideoGPT) in aligned experimental settings
Clear presentation with well-motivated visualizations and effective explanation of key concepts
Simple, practical techniques (experience rehearsal and execution guidance) that are straightforward to implement and integrate into existing RL systems
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: individual components are not new—experience rehearsal is standard nearest-neighbor retrieval, execution guidance mixes behavioral cloning with RL (similar to JSRL), and world model uses standard RSSM with minor modifications

Oversimplified retrieval method using only L2 distance on initial observations (Eq. 5); retrieval precision issues on some tasks (Door Open: 68% at top-500); no exploration of more sophisticated retrieval strategies or trajectory-level similarity
Theoretical analysis is incremental: Proposition 1 trivially states similar data has smaller distance; Proposition 2 directly applies Kakade & Langford (2002) without novel insights

Dataset labeled as 'non-curated' but remains in-domain: DMControl data from domain-specific unsupervised RL agents, Meta-World data from controlled corruption of task-specific policies—significantly limits claimed practical applicability to truly in-the-wild scenarios

Potentially unfair baseline comparisons: baselines receive only task-relevant pre-processed offline data while NCRL accesses full multi-embodiment dataset; preprocessing may artificially harm baseline performance

Incomplete analysis of task characteristics and method applicability: method performs poorly on some manipulation tasks (Pick Place: 0.20, Reach: 0.40, Soccer: 0.16 success rates); limited discussion of when/why approach succeeds

Limited generalization analysis: continual learning tested only on single embodiment; no evaluation of true cross-embodiment transfer or generalization to new embodiments acknowledged as incomplete in Section D
Computational overhead not addressed: retrieval requires pre-computing/storing encoder features for ~60k trajectories and FAISS indexing; no wall-clock time comparisons provided
Behavioral cloning quality unexplored: πbc trained on potentially limited retrieved data; no analysis of BC success rates or adaptive switching strategies
Missing ablations on key hyperparameters: number of retrieved trajectories R and offline data mix ratio not systematically evaluated
